blocks.content: Imagine you're starting a new project from scratch, and before writing a single line of business logic, you spend your first full day writing an XML file that tells the framework which class maps to which database table, an XML file that tells it which URL maps to which controller, and a third file that tells it where to find your templates.

By the end of the day you've written zero features and three configuration files, none of which do anything interesting on their own they just tell the framework facts that, if you'd named your files and classes in a predictable way to begin with, it could have figured out by itself.

A senior engineer glances at your screen and says: "Why are you telling it that UserControllerhandles /users? Just name it UserController and put it where controllers go it'll know." That's the entire idea behind convention over configuration: a framework that assumes the common, predictable case by default, and only asks you to write configuration for the cases where you genuinely deviate from it.
Most of this configuration exists only to describe patterns that are already obvious from the project's structure and naming conventions.

Convention Over Configuration was introduced to remove this repetitive work. Instead of forcing developers to explicitly configure every detail, the framework assumes sensible defaults and automatically follows common conventions.
This allows developers to focus on building application logic rather than writing configuration files.

A Real-Life Analogy Before Any Code

Think of a hotel room.

When you enter a standard hotel room, you already know where most things will be. The bed is usually in the center, the bathroom is nearby, and the light switches are close to the door. The hotel doesn't need to give every guest a detailed instruction manual because the layout follows a common convention.

Only when you want something different a connecting room, an extra bed, or a custom arrangement do you need to make a special request.

Convention Over Configuration works the same way.

A framework assumes common patterns and naming conventions by default. If you follow those conventions, everything works automatically. Configuration is only required when you want behavior that differs from the standard convention.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: 1. What Is Convention Over Configuration?

Convention Over Configuration (CoC) is a design principle where a framework automatically assumes sensible defaults based on naming conventions and project structure, reducing the amount of configuration developers need to write.
Instead of explicitly defining every mapping, relationship, and file location, the framework follows predefined conventions and infers the correct behavior automatically.
Configuration is only required when an application needs to behave differently from those defaults.
2. Why Naming Conventions Matter
Convention Over Configuration only works because naming conventions are consistent and predictable.
For example, a framework can automatically recognize UserController as a controller for user-related requests because it expects controllers to follow a standard naming pattern and location.
If every developer used different naming styles, the framework would have no reliable way to determine what each class represents. Every mapping would need to be configured manually.
This is why naming conventions and Convention Over Configuration go hand in hand
3. Real-Life Example: The Project From the Story
blocks.text: 3. Real-Life Example: The Project From the Story

blocks.content: Let's return to the project from the introduction. Instead of creating configuration files to map URLs, controllers, and database tables, we'll rely entirely on the framework's conventions.
How the Framework Infers a Route
blocks.text: How the Framework Infers a Route

blocks.content: When a request arrives for GET /users, the framework does not look inside a route configuration file. Instead, it follows its built-in conventions.
It searches the controllers folder for a controller that matches the request. Because a class named UserController exists, the framework automatically maps the /users request to that controller.
No XML mapping, route configuration, or manual setup is required. The framework infers the relationship from the class name and project structure alone.
In other words:

GET /users
        ↓
Framework Convention Rules
        ↓
UserController
The name itself becomes the configuration.
How Conventions Connect Components
The same principle applies beyond routing.

The framework sees a class named UserController and assumes it handles user-related requests. It then sees a model named User and assumes the controller works with user data. Finally, it infers that the User model maps to a database table named users.
No mapping file is needed to connect these pieces together.
The framework automatically creates the following relationships:

UserController
        ↓
User Model
        ↓
users Table
Because every component follows a predictable naming convention, the framework can discover how the application is structured without requiring explicit configuration.
This means:

UserController → handles user requests
User → represents user data
users → inferred database table

What Configuration Would Look Like Without Conventions

/users → UserController

User → users table 

UserController → User model

With Convention Over Configuration, the framework already knows these relationships as long as the naming conventions are followed.
Follow the framework's conventions, and the framework automatically discovers how the pieces fit together. Configuration is only needed when you want to break the convention.
4. Understanding the Code

Let's see how Convention Over Configuration reduces boilerplate by allowing the framework to infer routes, controllers, and database mappings automatically from naming conventions and project structure.

In this approach, every route must be configured manually. As the application grows, developers need to keep adding new mappings for every controller and endpoint. The framework knows nothing by default, so every relationship must be explicitly declared.
The framework sees a controller named UserController and a base route of /users. Using its built-in conventions, it automatically handles requests such as:

GET /users
GET /users/1
without requiring a separate route configuration file.

The framework sees a model named User and automatically assumes it should map to a database table named user (or users, depending on framework conventions). No explicit table mapping is needed because the naming convention already provides enough information.
Notice how only a small amount of information is provided:

UserController
User
/users
From these names, the framework automatically infers:

/users  → UserController
UserController → User
User → Database Table

blocks.content: This is Convention Over Configuration in practice.
Instead of describing every relationship manually, developers follow the framework's conventions and let the framework discover the rest automatically.
5. The Trade-Off

Like every design principle, Convention Over Configuration involves a trade-off. It reduces the amount of configuration developers need to write, but it also requires everyone to understand the framework's conventions.
1. What You Gain

["Less boilerplate code: Most common scenarios work automatically without extensive configuration.
","Predictable project structure: Developers can quickly find controllers, models, and other components because they follow standard conventions.
","Fewer configuration mistakes: Many routing and mapping errors disappear because relationships are inferred automatically.
"]
items: Less boilerplate code: Most common scenarios work automatically without extensive configuration.
Predictable project structure: Developers can quickly find controllers, models, and other components because they follow standard conventions.
Fewer configuration mistakes: Many routing and mapping errors disappear because relationships are inferred automatically.

blocks.content: 2. What You Pay

["Framework conventions must be learned: Some behavior is inferred behind the scenes, so developers need to understand the framework's rules.
","Custom behavior can require extra work: When you want to break a convention, additional configuration is often needed.
","Debugging may involve checking conventions: A naming mistake or incorrect folder placement can prevent the framework from finding a component automatically."]
items: Framework conventions must be learned: Some behavior is inferred behind the scenes, so developers need to understand the framework's rules.
Custom behavior can require extra work: When you want to break a convention, additional configuration is often needed.
Debugging may involve checking conventions: A naming mistake or incorrect folder placement can prevent the framework from finding a component automatically.

blocks.content: 6. Common Mistakes

["Breaking Conventions Unnecessarily: Using non-standard names and then adding configuration to make things work defeats the purpose of Convention Over Configuration.
","Fighting the Framework: Constantly overriding the framework's defaults often results in more configuration and complexity than simply following the established conventions.
","Assuming Configuration Is Never Needed: Convention Over Configuration reduces configuration, but it does not eliminate it. Real exceptions still require explicit configuration.
","Not Teaching the Conventions: Because much of the behavior is inferred automatically, new developers need to understand the framework's conventions to work effectively.
"]
items: Breaking Conventions Unnecessarily: Using non-standard names and then adding configuration to make things work defeats the purpose of Convention Over Configuration.
Fighting the Framework: Constantly overriding the framework's defaults often results in more configuration and complexity than simply following the established conventions.
Assuming Configuration Is Never Needed: Convention Over Configuration reduces configuration, but it does not eliminate it. Real exceptions still require explicit configuration.
Not Teaching the Conventions: Because much of the behavior is inferred automatically, new developers need to understand the framework's conventions to work effectively.

blocks.content: 7. Quick Reference

["Convention Over Configuration: Follow standard naming and project structure so the framework can infer behavior automatically.
","Hotel Room Analogy: A standard layout is assumed by default. Special requests only happen when you need something different.
","Relies on Naming Conventions: The framework can only make assumptions when names and structure are predictable.
","Benefits: Less boilerplate, consistent project structure, and fewer configuration errors.
","Trade-Offs: Developers must learn the framework's conventions, and debugging may require checking naming and folder structure.
","Remember: Configuration is still available for exceptions the goal is to reduce configuration for common cases, not eliminate it completely."]
items: Convention Over Configuration: Follow standard naming and project structure so the framework can infer behavior automatically.
Hotel Room Analogy: A standard layout is assumed by default. Special requests only happen when you need something different.
Relies on Naming Conventions: The framework can only make assumptions when names and structure are predictable.
Benefits: Less boilerplate, consistent project structure, and fewer configuration errors.
Trade-Offs: Developers must learn the framework's conventions, and debugging may require checking naming and folder structure.
Remember: Configuration is still available for exceptions the goal is to reduce configuration for common cases, not eliminate it completely.
